memory_leads.lead: Stevedores and terminal operating teams form the physical ship-shore cargo-execution layer; vessel crew retains shipboard safety and acceptance responsibilities, so productivity and damage can depend on an operational responsibility interface rather than one actor.

A stowage plan translates bookings or cargo parcels into bays, holds, decks or tanks subject to discharge sequence, weight, segregation, stability, structural and access constraints; the plan is an operational state, not merely paperwork.

Hatch and hold sequencing can determine whether gangs and cranes work in parallel or serially; an apparently available berth may deliver low effective throughput when the vessel-side work sequence is constrained.
Bulk trimming and distribution inside holds affect safe carriage, unloading access and vessel condition; trimming is a distinct execution step beyond simply loading the booked tonnage.
Dunnage, separation materials and parcel segregation protect cargo and preserve identity between lots; poor separation can create contamination, damage and later survey disputes.

Lashing and cargo securing are a dedicated execution chain involving securing plans, fittings, gangs or crew, inspection and re-tightening or monitoring; failure can become a safety, cargo-loss and schedule event.

Container operations rely on a specialized securing system of cells/guides and detachable fittings or rods; structural recall supports a lashing/securing category while exact equipment generations and rule tables remain deferred.

Reefer handling extends beyond stowage to plug availability, power continuity, settings/monitoring and exception response across terminal and vessel; a box can be physically loaded while its temperature-control service remains operationally incomplete.

Dangerous-goods execution depends on declared hazard identity, segregation/stowage constraints, documentation and emergency information; exact classes and current code provisions are deferred, but incompatible placement can constrain usable vessel or terminal capacity.

Bulk-cargo physical hazards such as excessive moisture or cargo behavior under motion can turn acceptance, loading or voyage safety into a cargo-readiness problem; exact commodity thresholds and code clauses require Evidence.

Heavy-lift and project cargo require lift planning, rigging, lifting points, crane radius/capacity, spreaders or slings and landing/securing preparation; one lift can become the critical path despite otherwise normal berth operations.
Ro-Ro cargo execution adds ramp availability, traffic sequencing, deck allocation and vehicle or trailer securing as a distinct handling topology from lift-on/lift-off cargo.

Ship cranes, derricks or other onboard cargo gear versus shore cranes create different maintenance, certification, operator and failure interfaces; crane or gear outage can reduce effective berth capacity without changing nominal berth or ship availability.

Stability, trim and structural-load constraints refine the atlas distinction between nominal and effective capacity: cargo may fit commercially but not be loadable in the desired sequence or distribution without violating vessel-side operating limits.

Cargo readiness is a port-call state separate from berth readiness: missing cargo, documentation, segregation preparation, equipment or receiving space can idle ship and gang despite an assigned berth.

Weather sensitivity is service-specific: wind can stop cranes, rain can stop moisture-sensitive cargo, and sea/swell can constrain exposed or offshore cargo work; a generic port-open/closed flag loses physical execution detail.

Stevedore or cargo-gear damage records feed the P013 survey/claims evidence chain, but the earlier causal state belongs here: handling method, equipment contact, sequence and securing choices are physical execution provenance.
The broad claim that gang, crane and berth productivity changes effective fleet capacity is already represented by atlas port-bottleneck/effective-capacity memory and prior port-service passes.
The general need for contemporaneous damage evidence is already covered by P013; this pass does not duplicate the downstream claims-survey chain.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Structural hazard and segregation concepts are recalled, but exact code editions, class tables, thresholds and legal applicability require Evidence.
Blind recall cannot support a reliable historical company/terminal productivity directory and such ranking would drift from mechanism-first coverage.
Exact local work rules, gang composition, shift arrangements, rates and tariffs vary by port and period and are deferred.
Many cargoes have specialized procedures, but blind enumeration would become a commodity manual rather than a bounded shipping-memory frontier.

stop_reason: The ship-shore physical cargo-execution chain is structurally populated; further recall is increasingly terminal-, commodity-, labor-rule-, equipment-model- or code-specific.

method_observation.observation: Port cargo productivity is better recalled as a sequence of compatible ship, terminal, cargo, equipment and safety states than as a single berth or crane productivity number.

truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no terminal practice, cargo rule, handling standard, productivity figure, company conduct or historical fact is verified.
